rubric.task_read: The agent must reverse-engineer an undocumented custom VLIW SIMD ISA and its simulator (problem.py), understand the kernel's computation well enough to preserve correctness, then rewrite kernel.py to go from 147,734 cycles to under 1,250 — a ~118x speedup — while staying correct across randomized inputs and honoring slot limits and the 'no cheating' rules. This is an extremely long-horizon, high-difficulty optimization task where success hinges on deep orientation, staged decomposition (correct→vectorized→bundle-packed→pipelined), a self-built verification loop, and quantitative reasoning about where cycles go. Nearly every meta-work faculty is exercised near its ceiling.

dimensions.name: ISA / simulator / problem reverse-engineering
dimensions.description: Understanding the VLIW ISA, the simulator's cost model, slot limits, hash stages, and the actual computation the kernel performs — before and while optimizing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Nothing here is documented for the agent's convenience; the ISA, how bundles are costed, SLOT_LIMITS, and the reference computation must be extracted from problem.py and the reference kernel. Every optimization decision and every correctness guarantee depends on an accurate model of the machine. Acting on a guessed ISA guarantees wasted cycles or wrong results.

anchors.0: Starts editing kernel.py without reading problem.py or the reference kernel; guesses at instructions.
anchors.3: Skims problem.py; identifies a few opcodes but misunderstands the cost model or slot limits; no grasp of what the kernel actually computes.
anchors.5: Reads problem.py and the reference kernel; correctly identifies the available ops, how cycles are counted per bundle, SLOT_LIMITS, and the high-level computation (forest/rounds/hash-stages) — enough to start correctly.
anchors.8: Builds a precise, explicit model: which slots/units exist, per-bundle cost rules, data dependencies in the hash stages, SIMD width, and the exact contract the reference kernel satisfies; probes the simulator with small experiments to confirm ambiguous behavior.
anchors.10: Derives a near-complete operational spec of the machine — instruction latencies, slot contention, what limits parallelism — and ties it directly to a theoretical cycle floor, re-probing the simulator whenever behavior surprises them; orientation is deep, experiment-driven, and continuously refined as optimization exposes new unknowns.

dimensions.name: Staged optimization plan with correctness gates
dimensions.description: Breaking the 118x effort into an ordered sequence of milestones (e.g. correct baseline → vectorize batch → pack bundles to slot limits → software-pipeline), each with a defined cycle/correctness checkpoint.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A single undifferentiated 'make it fast' push against a 118x gap thrashes. The task naturally decomposes into progressively more aggressive transforms, each of which must be landed and measured before the next. Ordering (correctness first, then coarse wins, then fine scheduling) is what keeps the work tractable.

anchors.0: No structure; edits ad hoc, chasing whatever comes to mind, mixing correctness and speed changes in one blob.
anchors.3: Vague intent to 'vectorize and pack bundles' but no ordered milestones or per-stage targets; changes are entangled.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered plan: get a correct rewrite, then vectorize across the batch, then pack bundles, verifying at each step, with a rough cycle target per stage.
anchors.8: Clear milestone hierarchy each with an explicit done-check and expected cycle impact; correctness-preserving transforms sequenced so each is independently measurable and revertible; the plan reflects the machine's actual bottlenecks.
anchors.10: A milestone structure that maps each stage to an estimated cycle contribution against a budget toward <1250, sequenced by expected payoff and risk, adjusted as measurements reveal which stages actually dominate — the decomposition itself evolves with evidence rather than being fixed upfront.

dimensions.name: Correctness verification beyond the canonical test
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing checks that the kernel stays correct across randomized inputs (not just the canonical case) and that each optimization preserves semantics, using run_tests.sh and self-built checks.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires correctness on randomized inputs; aggressive VLIW/SIMD transforms are easy to get subtly wrong (off-by-one lanes, wrong slot, stale register). Without a habit of re-verifying after each transform and against varied inputs, the agent can chase a low cycle count that silently fails the hidden correctness bar.

anchors.0: Never runs run_tests.sh, or only checks the cycle number and ignores correctness; assumes transforms are safe.
anchors.3: Runs the provided test occasionally; treats a single canonical pass as proof; no thought to randomized-input robustness.
anchors.5: Runs run_tests.sh after significant changes, confirms both correctness and cycles, and re-checks after each optimization stage.
anchors.8: Verifies after every semantic-affecting change and builds additional checks (e.g. comparing kernel output to the reference on self-generated varied inputs, isolating a transform to confirm it alone preserved results) rather than trusting the canonical case.
anchors.10: Runs a disciplined verification regime: diff-against-reference on many self-constructed edge inputs, per-transform correctness isolation, and guards against the specific ways VLIW scheduling can corrupt state — catching correctness regressions the provided test would miss before they compound.

dimensions.name: Cycle-count trajectory and thrash detection
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of current cycles vs the 1250 target, which optimizations landed, and detecting when effort has stalled or is circling.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Over a long optimization with many transforms, the agent must know its exact standing against the target, which changes helped, and when it is stuck re-trying variants that don't move the number. Losing this picture leads to repeating failed attempts or declaring victory prematurely.

anchors.0: No tracking of cycle counts over time; can't say whether recent changes helped or hurt.
anchors.3: Notices the current number but keeps no history; occasionally repeats changes already tried.
anchors.5: Tracks cycle count across attempts and knows distance to the 1250 target and roughly which change produced which gain.
anchors.8: Maintains a clear ledger of transform→cycle-delta, recognizes when a line of attack has plateaued, and redirects effort instead of grinding; distinguishes 'done enough' from 'more headroom' deliberately.
anchors.10: Continuously reconciles measured cycles against an expected budget per milestone, promptly flags stalls/circular debugging, and reallocates effort to the highest-remaining-payoff bottleneck — never loses the plot across a very long trajectory or churns on exhausted approaches.

dimensions.name: Revising approach when transforms fail or mislead
dimensions.description: Changing the optimization plan or ISA model when a transform breaks correctness, fails to reduce cycles as predicted, or reveals a wrong assumption about the machine.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A 118x speedup will involve dead ends: an optimization that the cost model predicted would help but doesn't, or that violates a slot limit or the anti-cheating rules. The agent must revert cleanly and rethink rather than barrel ahead on a falsified assumption or entrench a broken change.

anchors.0: Ignores contradictory results; keeps pushing a broken or ineffective approach; never reverts.
anchors.3: Reacts to failures by patching symptoms without questioning the underlying assumption; reverts messily or not at all.
anchors.5: When a change breaks correctness or doesn't help, backs it out and tries a different tactic; updates understanding of the machine when surprised.
anchors.8: Treats a falsified prediction as a signal to revise the cost model and plan; reverts cleanly, diagnoses why the expectation was wrong, and redirects — avoiding both sunk-cost persistence and flailing.
anchors.10: Systematically converts surprises into corrected machine models and re-sequenced plans; recognizes when a whole strategy (not just a transform) is wrong and pivots decisively, while preserving hard-won correct state — sustained, evidence-driven course-correction across the full effort.

dimensions.name: Quantitative cost modeling toward the cycle budget
dimensions.description: Building a quantitative model of where cycles are spent and what the theoretical floor is (given slot limits, SIMD width, dependency chains), and using it to target the <1250 budget.
dimensions.why_it_matters: This is an aggressive numeric target, not a vague 'faster'. Reaching <1250 from 147,734 requires reasoning about the achievable lower bound — how many bundles the computation must take given parallelism and slot constraints — to know which optimizations can possibly close the gap and when the agent is near the floor. This quantitative bottleneck analysis is distinct from generic progress tracking or correctness checking.

anchors.0: Optimizes blindly with no notion of where cycles go or what's achievable.
anchors.3: Hand-wavy sense that 'vectorizing helps' without quantifying the dominant cost or any floor.
anchors.5: Identifies the dominant cycle consumers (e.g. per-round hash-stage work × batch) and reasons roughly about how much a transform can save.
anchors.8: Constructs an explicit cost model tying instruction counts and slot occupancy to cycles, estimates a theoretical lower bound, and uses the gap between measured and floor to prioritize the next optimization.
anchors.10: Derives a tight lower-bound cycle model from slot limits, SIMD width, and critical-path dependencies, uses it to decide which transforms are worth attempting and to recognize when the kernel is near-optimal — turning a blind search into a directed descent toward the budget.
